name: Protocol Buffers
summary: A schema-driven serialization system whose numbered, typed wire records support generated APIs, unknown-field handling, and constrained schema evolution.

features.name: Tagged self-delimiting wire format
features.description: Protocol Buffers encodes messages as field tags and values. The tag combines a field number with a wire type, and the wire type determines how the decoder consumes the value. The fixed source implements skipping for varints, fixed-width values, length-delimited values, groups, and invalid field numbers.
benefits: Decoders can consume fields without knowing every field definition
costs: Field numbers and wire types become compatibility-critical
The wire format does not carry field names or declared types
Recursive and length-delimited parsing needs resource controls

features.name: Unknown-field skipping and preservation
features.description: The wire-format implementation can skip fields it does not interpret and copy skipped field bytes to an unknown-field output. The official guide describes unknown fields as newer fields encountered by older binaries and documents their retention in binary parsing and serialization.
benefits: Older readers can survive additive fields
Binary relays can preserve forward data
Wire compatibility is separated from generated API knowledge
costs: Unknown data can be lost across JSON, text, or field-by-field transformations
Applications must still coordinate semantic meaning
Opaque bytes add memory and serialization work

features.name: Descriptor-driven generated code
features.description: The compiler plugin builds descriptors for requested proto files, checks that requested files have descriptors, creates a response context, and exposes generated output files through the plugin response. Official documentation describes protoc as generating language-specific message and serialization APIs.
benefits: One schema contract can serve supported languages
Repetitive serialization and API glue is generated
costs: Generated APIs vary by language and runtime
Schema changes require compiler and artifact coordination

features.name: Numbered schema evolution contract
features.description: Protocol Buffers treats field numbers as stable wire identifiers. The official guide documents additive fields and removal as binary wire-safe when numbers are not reused, while changing existing numbers is wire-unsafe and deleted numbers should be reserved.
benefits: Compatibility constraints are reviewable at the schema boundary
Old and new generated code can exchange a shared binary format
costs: Schema history must retain reserved identifiers
Wire-compatible changes can still break application code
JSON and text mappings have different compatibility rules

mathematical_views.model: Tagged message stream with partial schema interpretation
mathematical_views.question: How can a reader decode known fields while safely advancing over fields outside its schema?
assumptions: Each tag identifies a valid field number and wire type
Wire types provide enough information to consume a record without its source-level name
Unknown retention is modeled as an opaque side channel

mathematical_views.model: Schema evolution as a constrained refinement relation
mathematical_views.question: Which schema edits preserve binary parsing behavior across old and new readers?
assumptions: Field numbers remain stable and deleted identifiers are not reused
The question is limited to documented binary wire behavior
Application validation and generated-language exhaustiveness are separate

mathematical_views.question: How does a proto schema become language-specific generated artifacts through compiler plugins?
assumptions: A plugin response identifies output files and contents

benefits: Unknown values can be skipped by type
costs: Parsing is stateful for recursive values

benefits: Improves forward compatibility of binary relays
costs: Opaque data handling is format-boundary sensitive
Builds depend on plugin and generated-artifact freshness
Identifier reservation is permanent maintenance work
